item.title: Biodiversity and the Conferences of the Parties
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 16 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02792-w

In a year containing summits from the three United Nations environmental frameworks, we consider how cooperation across the Conferences of the Parties (COPs) can facilitate implementation and impact. Co-timed with the start of the biodiversity COP, we highlight the reciprocal relationship between climate change and biodiversity.
item.dc:title: Biodiversity and the Conferences of the Parties

item.title: Astrid Schomaker on biodiversity in a triple COP year
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 16 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02778-8

This year, all three major Rio Conventions — on biodiversity, climate and desertification — convene their respective Conference of the Parties (COP). In advance of the biodiversity COP17, Astrid Schomaker, the executive secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity, discusses the irrefutable need to integrate biodiversity conservation into broader environmental action to ensure local and global security and prosperity in a rapidly changing world.
item.dc:title: Astrid Schomaker on biodiversity in a triple COP year
item.dc:creator: Tegan Armarego-Marriott

item.title: Climate choices and attention are shaped more by politics than weather
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 16 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02775-x

Climate change will further increase the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events. Subjective experience and attribution of extreme weather events to climate change, rather than objective exposure alone, are associated with greater climate-relevant attention and choices. Political affiliation influences attention and behaviour irrespective of subjective attribution and objective exposure.
item.dc:title: Climate choices and attention are shaped more by politics than weather

item.title: Political affiliation impacts climate attention and choice beyond extreme weather exposure
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 16 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02765-z

Mechanisms behind climate decision-making remain unclear. This study shows that political affiliation and subjective attribution shape attention allocation and climate-related choices, with subjective attribution moderating the effects of political affiliation and objective weather exposure.
item.dc:title: Political affiliation impacts climate attention and choice beyond extreme weather exposure

item.title: Combining climate policy instruments for a just transition to a climate-neutral economy
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02757-z

A distributional analysis of European Union climate policy pathways traces the costs of reducing carbon dioxide emissions to the level of households based on their spending and income patterns. We find that different equity considerations, including income inequality and within-group impact divergence, can shape optimal climate policy design with carbon prices, transfers, standards and subsidies.
item.dc:title: Combining climate policy instruments for a just transition to a climate-neutral economy

item.title: Warming oceans hit the battlefield
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02782-y

Marine radar signal propagation is highly sensitive to fine-scale vertical changes in water vapour. Now research shows that long-term increases in sea surface temperatures are strengthening the frequency and intensity of the features that allow radar signals to travel further than expected.
item.dc:title: Warming oceans hit the battlefield
item.dc:creator: David D. Flagg

item.title: Warming-driven lower-tropospheric stratification intensifies ducting over global oceans
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02774-y

Atmospheric ducts are waveguides that affect electromagnetic propagation in the atmosphere, affecting radar and other technologies. Here the authors show that warming intensifies such ducting over mid- to low-latitude oceans.
item.dc:title: Warming-driven lower-tropospheric stratification intensifies ducting over global oceans

item.title: High wind speed reduces water use efficiency across terrestrial ecosystems
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02781-z

The role of wind in ecosystem water use efficiency remains unclear. The authors show that water use efficiency declines with increasing wind speed, driven mainly by increases in evapotranspiration and secondarily by reductions in gross primary productivity.
item.dc:title: High wind speed reduces water use efficiency across terrestrial ecosystems

item.title: Prioritizing demand-side use of clean hydrogen for cost-effective mitigation
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02763-1

Clean hydrogen is widely proposed for hard-to-abate sector decarbonization, but its limited supply requires prioritizing sectors with the highest value. This study evaluates ten sectors and identifies key no-regret uses, while highlighting the need for specific demand-side policies.
item.dc:title: Prioritizing demand-side use of clean hydrogen for cost-effective mitigation

item.title: The ambitions and limitations of climate assemblies
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02764-0

Climate citizens’ assemblies are gaining traction worldwide as a way to involve the public in climate governance. Now a study demonstrates that although these assemblies propose more ambitious recommendations than existing climate policy, these recommendations vary across contexts and have limited impact on policy decisions.
item.dc:title: The ambitions and limitations of climate assemblies
item.dc:creator: Amanda Machin

item.title: Strengthening Rio Convention implementation architecture through reciprocal learning
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02777-9

As the Rio Conventions mature from negotiating commitments towards delivering them, strengthening implementation has become an urgent priority. We argue for greater cross-convention learning within the context of institutional architecture to accelerate progress on climate, biodiversity and land degradation.
item.dc:title: Strengthening Rio Convention implementation architecture through reciprocal learning
item.dc:creator: Hollie Folkard-Tapp
Jennifer Lenhart
Benjamin Parker
Nathalie Pettorelli

item.title: Citizens’ assemblies propose ambitious climate policy but impacts remain limited
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02755-1

Deliberative citizen participation, such as climate assemblies, has been promoted in climate governance. This study finds that, although assemblies proposed more ambitious recommendations than existing climate policy, these recommendations rarely translated into actual policy decisions.
item.dc:title: Citizens’ assemblies propose ambitious climate policy but impacts remain limited

item.title: Enhancing fairness in climate action through policy packages
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 13 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02751-5

Achieving climate neutrality requires policies perceived as fair, with equity both between and within income groups. Here researchers evaluate the equity implications of different European Union climate policy packages and show how a mixed policy design can balance trade-offs between two equity dimensions.
item.dc:title: Enhancing fairness in climate action through policy packages
